actions.name: Disseminated TrickBot and BazarLoader via phishing campaigns
actions.description: Cybercriminals disseminate TrickBot and BazarLoader via phishing campaigns that contain either links to malicious websites that host the malware or attachments with the malware.

actions.name: Executed TrickBot malware on victim machine
actions.description: After successful execution of the malware, TrickBot copies itself as an executable file with a 12-character (includes .exe), randomly generated file name and places this file in one of the following directories: C:\Windows\, C:\Windows\SysWOW64\, or C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\.

actions.name: Established persistence via scheduled tasks
actions.description: The malware uses scheduled tasks that run every 15 minutes to ensure persistence on the victim machine. The scheduled task typically uses the naming convention: [random_folder_name_in_%APPDATA%_excluding_Microsoft] autoupdate#[5_random_numbers] (e.g., Task autoupdate#16876).

actions.name: Deployed malicious batch scripts using PowerShell commands
actions.description: After successful execution, anchor_dns further deploys malicious batch scripts (.bat) using PowerShell commands.

actions.name: Executed self-deletion commands
actions.description: The malware deploys self-deletion techniques by executing commands such as 'cmd.exe /c timeout 3 && del C:\Users\[username]\[malware_sample]' and 'cmd.exe /C PowerShell "Start-Sleep 3; Remove-Item C:\Users\[username]\[malware_sample_location]\"'.

actions.name: Delivered BazarLoader malware via phishing emails
actions.description: Deployment of the BazarLoader malware typically comes from phishing email delivered by commercial mass email delivery services containing links to actor-controlled Google Drive documents or other free online filehosting solutions, typically purporting to be a PDF file, which then link to malware payloads.

actions.name: Mapped network and enumerated environment using native tools
actions.description: Ryuk actors map the network to enumerate the environment using native tools such as net view, net computers, and ping to locate mapped network shares, domain controllers, and active directory.

actions.name: Moved laterally using native and third-party tools
actions.description: Ryuk actors move laterally throughout the network using native tools such as PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), Windows Remote Management, and Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), as well as third-party tools like Bloodhound.

actions.name: Encrypted files using Ryuk ransomware
actions.description: Ryuk uses AES-256 to encrypt files and an RSA public key to encrypt the AES key. Files have been encrypted with their own AES key and given a file extension of .RYK. Encrypted directories have had a ransom note of RyukReadMe.txt written to the directory.

actions.name: Deleted volume shadow copies and backups
actions.description: Ryuk uses commands such as vssadmin Delete Shadows /all /quiet and vssadmin resize shadowstorage to delete volume shadow copies and backups to inhibit system recovery.

actions.name: Stopped or disabled security services
actions.description: Ryuk attackers attempt to shut down or uninstall security applications on victim systems that might prevent ransomware execution, normally via scripts but also manually if needed.

actions.name: Established persistence via scheduled tasks and registry run keys
actions.description: Ryuk actors have been known to use scheduled tasks and create Registry entries under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to maintain persistence.
